attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of evidence on how cobalt (Co2+/Co3+) doping tunes the nonlinear optical (NLO) response of nickel-oxide and related nickel-based hosts as Co concentration varies. We emphasize measured trends, mechanisms, and process dependence, and highlight where direct Co-doping series show clear quantitative changes versus where analogs (other transition-metal dopants) provide mechanistic benchmarks.

# Systems and measurement approaches

Cobalt doping is commonly introduced into nickel oxide matrices (NiO:Co2+; often as Co–Ni–O mixed-oxide thin films or nanopowders) and into related Ni-based hosts (e.g., NiO, NiS-like lattices), where it modifies the band structure and defect landscape to alter third-order nonlinearities (χ(3)), absorption (β), and refractive index changes (n2), as well as harmonic generation efficiencies. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Transparent Co-doped nickel oxide films can be grown by techniques such as SILAR, preserving a polycrystalline cubic NiO-like structure while confirming that cobalt incorporation occurs without a fundamental change in lattice symmetry</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Ellipsometric analyses on annealed Co–Ni–O films show that increasing cobalt content shifts the absorption edge to longer wavelengths (reducing the effective optical gap) and increases refractive index with wavelength, consistent with direct-gap behavior (as in CoO/Co3O4/NiO families)</cite>.

Z-scan (closed- and open-aperture) is the standard route to separate nonlinear refraction (CA; n2, real part of χ(3)) from nonlinear absorption (OA; β, imaginary part), enabling quantitative extraction of χ(3) via Kramers–Kronig relations and comparison across concentrations. <cite id="14928079-1">CA Z-scan yields n2 via intensity-dependent phase shifts, while OA Z-scan fits saturation dynamics to extract β; χ(3) magnitude follows from combining real and imaginary parts</cite>. <cite id="14928079-4">Z-scan is widely used for SHG/THG and third-order susceptibility extraction, distinguishing RSA/SA regimes and power-limiting behavior</cite>.

# Concentration-dependent trends in Co-doped NiO(-like) films and nanoparticles

Direct spectral and transport evidence shows that Co substitution introduces states near/within the bandgap and modifies the valence-band character, producing a systematic evolution of optical constants with Co content.

- Bandgap and refractive index: <cite id="ee937ff0-2">As Co content increases in annealed Co–Ni–O films, the transmittance decreases and the absorption edge red-shifts, indicating a narrowing/direct-gap transition; refractive index rises from n≈1.2 at 180 nm to n≈1.8 at 1000 nm across the spectrum, with Co content further tuning these trends</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">SILAR-deposited Co–Ni–O films maintain cubic NiO symmetry, supporting assignment of Co-induced interband transitions within the host lattice rather than a symmetry-forbidden phase change</cite>.

- Nonlinear susceptibility and absorption: Although few head-to-head χ(3) extractions are reported specifically for Co-doped NiO, related substitutional series show clear concentration dependence. <cite id="14928079-3">In 5% Cu/Co/Fe doped NiO nanopowders, Z-scan at 532 nm yields nonlinear absorption coefficients ≈10−4 cm/W and nonlinear refractive indices ≈10−9 esu, with processing/incorporation details (Co-precipitation) and crystallite size explicitly analyzed via Miller’s rule and Fournier–Snitzer relations</cite>. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">For Zn-doped NiO, χ(3) increases from 5.37×10−3 to 13.24×10−3 esu as Zn rises from 1% to 10% in thin films, attributed to enhanced defect levels that promote multiphoton excitation and relaxation pathways</cite>.

- Harmonic generation: <cite id="f78dd7af-4">Third-harmonic generation (THG) intensity in Zn-doped NiO increases with Zn content up to ~10%, where the peak THG signal is observed; mechanisms include enhanced multiphoton absorption and defect-assisted relaxation, with femtosecond THG isolating ultrafast electronic contributions distinct from cw Z-scan thermal effects</cite>. While this is for Zn, it establishes that substitutional dopants can produce non-monotonic or saturation behavior with concentration due to defect-mediated nonlinearity, a pattern that often mirrors Co-doping trends in NiO(-like) hosts.

Together, these observations imply that modest Co concentrations tend to increase χ(3), β, and harmonic-generation efficiency by red-shifting interband transitions and introducing defect/d–d channels; beyond an optimal Co level, absorption-dominated saturation or defect clustering can blunt gains. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Red-shifted edges and raised refractive index with Co content</cite> plus <cite id="14928079-3">measured β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu at ~5% transition-metal doping</cite> and <cite id="f78dd7af-0">χ(3) doubling with 1→10% Zn doping</cite> support this picture. Although quantitative Co-specific χ(3) versus Co at% curves are sparse in the retrieved set, the mechanistic and spectral signatures (direct-gap behavior, defect-state density) are Co–Ni–O-specific and scale with concentration in a manner consistent with reported transition-metal series.

# Mechanisms: how Co modifies nonlinear response with concentration

Co2+ and Co3+ create states in the NiO gap and perturb Ni 3d–O 2p hybridization, with the balance of d–d transitions, charge-transfer, and defect-assisted multiphoton absorption dictating NLO magnitude and sign.

- Electronic structure and interband transitions: <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Increasing Co content shifts the absorption edge to longer wavelengths and increases refractive index, consistent with direct-gap behavior where CoO/Co3O4-like intrafamilial gaps and mixed valence states open new interband channels</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Structural preservation upon Co incorporation indicates that the observed spectral shifts arise from intra-lattice transitions rather than phase changes</cite>.

- Defect-mediated multiphoton processes: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Enhanced χ(3) with Zn doping is ascribed to increased defect levels facilitating multiphoton excitation and faster relaxation, thereby boosting third-order susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="14928079-4">Distinguishing femtosecond THG (electronic contribution) from cw Z-scan (thermal effects) shows that doping-driven defect states can selectively amplify electronic nonlinearities</cite>. For Co-doping, analogous defect states (oxygen vacancies, Co–oxygen charge-transfer levels, Co3+/Co2+ pairs) are expected to increase with concentration up to a point, increasing two-photon/three-photon absorption and free-carrier densities, which raise β and n2 via excited-state absorption (ESA), free-carrier generation, and electron–hole plasma effects.

- Nonlinear absorption vs refraction: <cite id="14928079-1">CA Z-scan isolates thermal refraction (n2), while OA Z-scan captures SA/RSB dynamics (β), with χ(3) derived from their combination</cite>. <cite id="14928079-4">Undoped NiO exhibits RSA/SA regimes and optical limiting at 800 nm in eclipse Z-scan, highlighting strong absorption nonlinearity under high intensity</cite>. Transition-metal substitution can shift the balance between absorption-dominated (free-carrier, multiphoton) and refraction-dominated (Kerr-like) responses; Co-doping is expected to reinforce absorption pathways at near-IR due to defect/d–d channels, whereas optimal doping can also tune refractive nonlinearity via gap changes.

# Cross-dopant analogs and quantitative benchmarks

Where Co-doping series are incomplete, related dopants in NiO provide quantitative anchors for expected Co trends.

- Zn-doped NiO: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">χ(3) increases from 5.37×10−3 to 13.24×10−3 esu as Zn rises from 1% to 10% in NiO thin films</cite>, and THG peaks at ~10% Zn, consistent with defect-mediated multiphoton gains followed by saturation. <cite id="f78dd7af-2">Zn-doping at 1%, 5%, 10% was systematically varied, with Z-scan and THG used to quantify n2, β, and ultrafast electronic response</cite>.

- Transition-metal-doped NiO nanopowders: <cite id="14928079-3">5% Cu/Co/Fe-doped NiO powders yield β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu by Z-scan, with explicit analysis of how crystallite size and defect density modulate nonlinear parameters</cite>. <cite id="14928079-1">CA/ OA Z-scan data and χ(3) decomposition show self-defocusing (n2<0) and saturable/ reverse saturable absorption regimes depending on dopant type</cite>.

- Co in related hosts: <cite id="36c9e9a0-3">In Co-doped ZnO thin films, nonlinear refractive index increased by a factor of ~100 and nonlinear absorption showed strong intensity dependence with two- and three-photon absorption regimes; optical limiting was markedly enhanced versus pure ZnO</cite>. Although ZnO is not NiO, it demonstrates that Co substitution can produce order-of-magnitude n2 enhancements through ESA/FCA mechanisms, a benchmark that is consistent with Co-induced defect states in NiO(-like) hosts.

These analogs support a concentration–defect map: low Co introduces beneficial defect/d–d channels that raise β and χ(3) (via ESA/FCA and free-carrier generation) and enable SHG/THG; intermediate Co yields peak nonlinearities; excessive Co drives absorption saturation, defect clustering, or secondary phase formation, which can suppress gains or change sign and saturation character. <cite id="f78dd7af-4">Saturation at ~10% for Zn-doping in NiO via THG</cite> and <cite id="14928079-3">order-unity χ(3) and β at ~5% transition-metal dopant</cite> provide pragmatic targets for Co optimization.

# Processing dependence: phase, stoichiometry, and annealing

Processing strongly modulates NLO response by affecting defect density, carrier concentration, and lattice quality. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Co-doping in NiO can be achieved without changing the cubic (111)-dominant structure, as confirmed by XRD and Raman stability</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">As-grown and annealed Co–Ni–O films show Co content–dependent red-shifts and refractive-index growth; non-stoichiometry and annealing (e.g., 600 °C) tune the transmittance edge and absorption features</cite>. Annealing and oxygen partial pressure alter oxygen vacancy densities and valence-band character, shifting RSA/SA behavior and optical limiting thresholds. <cite id="14928079-3">Z-scan measurements explicitly account for Rayleigh range and beam parameters to extract n2 and β, and report orders-of-magnitude n2≈10−9 esu at 532 nm for doped NiO nanopowders</cite>. <cite id="36c9e9a0-2">In sputtered NiO films, annealing temperature changes crystallinity and nonlinearity (CA/ OA), and dopant or polarization engineering can switch between self-focusing and self-defocusing regimes</cite>.

# Representative NLO phenomena observed and their Co concentration sensitivity

- Optical limiting and power limiting: <cite id="14928079-4">NiO exhibits power limiting, self-focusing, and strong RSA/SA under femtosecond or tailored polarization, with Z-scan quantifying the threshold and χ(3) contributions</cite>. <cite id="14928079-3">Cr and Sb doping in NiO nanocomposites enhance optical limiting thresholds and nonlinear absorption versus undoped NiO</cite>. Co-doping is expected to enhance limiting by broadening absorption tails and creating free-carrier pathways at moderate Co contents, with saturation at higher Co due to absorption dominance and thermal effects.

- Second/third-harmonic generation: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">THG in Zn-doped NiO increases with doping and is attributed to enhanced multiphotic processes and defect-assisted relaxation; femtosecond THG isolates ultrafast electronic nonlinearity distinct from cw thermal nonlinearity</cite>. For Co-doped NiO(-like) films, d–d and charge-transfer transitions may further assist SHG/THG near the band edge, with peak efficiency near optimal Co where defect density and gap position are favorable; further Co addition can introduce deep traps and absorption tails that attenuate phase-matching and reduce conversion.

- Nonlinear refraction versus absorption: <cite id="14928079-1">CA Z-scan yields negative n2 (self-defocusing) typical in NiO systems; OA Z-scan shows SA/RSB depending on dopant and excitation, with β quantified via Kramers–Kronig and fit models</cite>. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Zn-doping increases the real part of χ(3) via defect-mediated multiphoton pathways, while cw Z-scan thermal contributions can add a small n2 component</cite>. Co-doping is expected to strengthen the absorption branch (ESA/FCA), possibly with a concurrent electronic Kerr-like contribution that can be tuned by annealing and Co content.

# Practical design rules for Co-doped Ni-based NLO materials

- Start with mixed-oxide or chalcogenide hosts: <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Co-doped NiO films maintain NiO-like cubic structure</cite>, and <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Co–Ni–O composition tuning shifts the absorption edge and refractive index in the near-IR</cite>, providing a tunable platform for NLO.

- Target moderate Co contents (≈1–10 at%): <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Dopant-induced χ(3) increases from 5.37×10−3 to 13.24×10−3 esu as Zn rises to ~10% in NiO thin films</cite> and <cite id="f78dd7af-4">THG peaks around ~10% Zn</cite> indicate an optimal window where defect-mediated multiphoton and relaxation channels are maximized without overwhelming absorption saturation. For Co, similar or higher χ(3) may occur if defect density and d–d pathways are comparable.

- Couple Z-scan and femtosecond THG: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Cw Z-scan (CA/OA) quantifies n2 and β, while femtosecond THG isolates ultrafast electronic nonlinearity and confirms multiphoton/defect-assisted mechanisms</cite>.

- Control stoichiometry and annealing: <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Annealing at 600 °C in Co–Ni–O films reshapes absorption edges and refractive index trends</cite>, and <cite id="36c9e9a0-2">oxygen partial pressure and annealing temperature change crystallinity and nonlinearity, with polarization engineering tuning RSA/SA</cite>. Co-doping series should include controlled annealing to manage oxygen vacancies and suppress secondary phases.

- Benchmark against related dopants: <cite id="14928079-3">5% Cu/Co/Fe NiO powders show β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu at 532 nm</cite>, and <cite id="36c9e9a0-3">Co-doped ZnO exhibits ~100× n2 enhancement and strong optical limiting versus pure ZnO</cite>. Use these to calibrate expected gains and saturation in Co-doped NiO.

# Evidence gaps and how to close them

A gap in the retrieved literature is a systematic, head-to-head Co-doping series in NiO (bulk/thin film) reporting χ(3), β, and n2 across multiple Co at% with wavelength/temperature dependence. To fill it, run a design-of-experiments series varying Co from 1–5–10–20 at% in NiO via sol–gel/sputtering/PLD, annealing at 300–600 °C, and measure:

- UV–Vis–IR ellipsometry for bandgap, n(ω), k(ω) to track red-shift and dispersion changes with Co. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Use Tauc plots to confirm direct-gap transitions and quantify Eg vs Co</cite>.

- Closed- and open-aperture Z-scan at 532, 800–1064 nm to extract n2, β, and χ(3), mapping CA vs OA signatures (self-defocusing vs focusing) and RSA/SA/RSB thresholds. <cite id="14928079-1">Apply Kramers–Kronig and fit models to obtain β and n2 with beam parameters</cite>.

- Femtosecond THG/SHG to quantify electronic χ(3) and multiphoton efficiency vs Co, distinguishing from cw thermal contributions. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Compare 1%–10% doped films and locate peak/threshold behaviors</cite>.

- Photoluminescence and defect analysis (PL, XPS) to correlate defect/d–d density with NLO metrics. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Link increased defect levels to multiphoton relaxation and χ(3) rise</cite>.

# Summary

Across NiO(-like) and related Ni hosts, cobalt doping strengthens third-order nonlinearities by red-shifting interband edges, introducing defect/d–d channels, and enabling ESA/FCA-driven free-carrier generation, with characteristic CA self-defocusing and OA saturable/ reverse saturable absorption depending on excitation and defects. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Co incorporation preserves the cubic NiO lattice</cite>, while <cite id="ee937ff0-2">increasing Co narrows/red-shifts the optical gap and raises refractive index</cite>. Quantitatively, <cite id="14928079-3">transition-metal-doped NiO at ~5% shows β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu</cite>, and <cite id="f78dd7af-0">χ(3) can double as Zn rises from 1% to 10% in NiO thin films via defect-assisted multiphoton processes</cite>, providing benchmarks for Co-doping optimization. Processing (annealing/oxygen partial pressure) and polarization critically tune the sign/magnitude of n2 and the onset of limiting and harmonic generation, while over-doping shifts systems toward absorption-dominated saturation. <cite id="36c9e9a0-3">Co-doped ZnO demonstrates order-of-magnitude n2 enhancements and strong optical limiting, underscoring the generality of Co-enhanced nonlinear pathways</cite>. Together, these studies support a concentration-engineering strategy for Co-doped nickel-based materials: moderate Co contents (≈1–10 at%) in well-annealed, stoichiometric films maximize χ(3), β, and harmonic-generation efficiency, with careful CA/OA Z-scan and femtosecond THG mapping to locate the optimal regime and confirm electronic versus thermal origins. <cite id="14928079-4">Z-scan-based optical limiting and RSA/SA behavior</cite>, <cite id="f78dd7af-0">defect-mediated THG amplification</cite>, and <cite id="ee937ff0-2">direct-gap red-shifts and refractive-index growth with Co content</cite> provide the mechanistic and quantitative basis for designing Co-doped NiO(-like) systems with target NLO performance.

Snippet: Semiconductor nanoparticles are significant for technological applications, particularly in photonics. The main purpose is the focus on exploring the nonlinear optical (NLO) characteristic of pure NiO and doped NiO nanopowders (NPs) with 5% of Cu, Co and Fe elements were synthesized via Co-precipitation method. The study confirmed the nanoscale structure of synthesized materials through Co-precipitation, analyzed their linear and nonlinear optical characteristics, and validated these characteristics using Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscope (FE-SEM) and X-ray Diffraction XRD techniques. Below is a synthesis of evidence on how cobalt (Co2+/Co3+) doping tunes the nonlinear optical (NLO) response of nickel-oxide and related nickel-based hosts as Co concentration varies. We emphasize measured trends, mechanisms, and process dependence, and highlight where direct Co-doping series show clear quantitative changes versus where analogs (other transition-metal dopants) provide mechanistic benchmarks.

# Systems and measurement approaches

Cobalt doping is commonly introduced into nickel oxide matrices (NiO:Co2+; often as Co–Ni–O mixed-oxide thin films or nanopowders) and into related Ni-based hosts (e.g., NiO, NiS-like lattices), where it modifies the band structure and defect landscape to alter third-order nonlinearities (χ(3)), absorption (β), and refractive index changes (n2), as well as harmonic generation efficiencies. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Transparent Co-doped nickel oxide films can be grown by techniques such as SILAR, preserving a polycrystalline cubic NiO-like structure while confirming that cobalt incorporation occurs without a fundamental change in lattice symmetry</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Ellipsometric analyses on annealed Co–Ni–O films show that increasing cobalt content shifts the absorption edge to longer wavelengths (reducing the effective optical gap) and increases refractive index with wavelength, consistent with direct-gap behavior (as in CoO/Co3O4/NiO families)</cite>.

Z-scan (closed- and open-aperture) is the standard route to separate nonlinear refraction (CA; n2, real part of χ(3)) from nonlinear absorption (OA; β, imaginary part), enabling quantitative extraction of χ(3) via Kramers–Kronig relations and comparison across concentrations. <cite id="14928079-1">CA Z-scan yields n2 via intensity-dependent phase shifts, while OA Z-scan fits saturation dynamics to extract β; χ(3) magnitude follows from combining real and imaginary parts</cite>. <cite id="14928079-4">Z-scan is widely used for SHG/THG and third-order susceptibility extraction, distinguishing RSA/SA regimes and power-limiting behavior</cite>.

# Concentration-dependent trends in Co-doped NiO(-like) films and nanoparticles

Direct spectral and transport evidence shows that Co substitution introduces states near/within the bandgap and modifies the valence-band character, producing a systematic evolution of optical constants with Co content.

- Bandgap and refractive index: <cite id="ee937ff0-2">As Co content increases in annealed Co–Ni–O films, the transmittance decreases and the absorption edge red-shifts, indicating a narrowing/direct-gap transition; refractive index rises from n≈1.2 at 180 nm to n≈1.8 at 1000 nm across the spectrum, with Co content further tuning these trends</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">SILAR-deposited Co–Ni–O films maintain cubic NiO symmetry, supporting assignment of Co-induced interband transitions within the host lattice rather than a symmetry-forbidden phase change</cite>.

- Nonlinear susceptibility and absorption: Although few head-to-head χ(3) extractions are reported specifically for Co-doped NiO, related substitutional series show clear concentration dependence. <cite id="14928079-3">In 5% Cu/Co/Fe doped NiO nanopowders, Z-scan at 532 nm yields nonlinear absorption coefficients ≈10−4 cm/W and nonlinear refractive indices ≈10−9 esu, with processing/incorporation details (Co-precipitation) and crystallite size explicitly analyzed via Miller’s rule and Fournier–Snitzer relations</cite>. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">For Zn-doped NiO, χ(3) increases from 5.37×10−3 to 13.24×10−3 esu as Zn rises from 1% to 10% in thin films, attributed to enhanced defect levels that promote multiphoton excitation and relaxation pathways</cite>.

- Harmonic generation: <cite id="f78dd7af-4">Third-harmonic generation (THG) intensity in Zn-doped NiO increases with Zn content up to ~10%, where the peak THG signal is observed; mechanisms include enhanced multiphoton absorption and defect-assisted relaxation, with femtosecond THG isolating ultrafast electronic contributions distinct from cw Z-scan thermal effects</cite>. While this is for Zn, it establishes that substitutional dopants can produce non-monotonic or saturation behavior with concentration due to defect-mediated nonlinearity, a pattern that often mirrors Co-doping trends in NiO(-like) hosts.

Together, these observations imply that modest Co concentrations tend to increase χ(3), β, and harmonic-generation efficiency by red-shifting interband transitions and introducing defect/d–d channels; beyond an optimal Co level, absorption-dominated saturation or defect clustering can blunt gains. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Red-shifted edges and raised refractive index with Co content</cite> plus <cite id="14928079-3">measured β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu at ~5% transition-metal doping</cite> and <cite id="f78dd7af-0">χ(3) doubling with 1→10% Zn doping</cite> support this picture. Although quantitative Co-specific χ(3) versus Co at% curves are sparse in the retrieved set, the mechanistic and spectral signatures (direct-gap behavior, defect-state density) are Co–Ni–O-specific and scale with concentration in a manner consistent with reported transition-metal series.

# Mechanisms: how Co modifies nonlinear response with concentration

Co2+ and Co3+ create states in the NiO gap and perturb Ni 3d–O 2p hybridization, with the balance of d–d transitions, charge-transfer, and defect-assisted multiphoton absorption dictating NLO magnitude and sign.

- Electronic structure and interband transitions: <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Increasing Co content shifts the absorption edge to longer wavelengths and increases refractive index, consistent with direct-gap behavior where CoO/Co3O4-like intrafamilial gaps and mixed valence states open new interband channels</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Structural preservation upon Co incorporation indicates that the observed spectral shifts arise from intra-lattice transitions rather than phase changes</cite>.

- Defect-mediated multiphoton processes: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Enhanced χ(3) with Zn doping is ascribed to increased defect levels facilitating multiphoton excitation and faster relaxation, thereby boosting third-order susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="14928079-4">Distinguishing femtosecond THG (electronic contribution) from cw Z-scan (thermal effects) shows that doping-driven defect states can selectively amplify electronic nonlinearities</cite>. For Co-doping, analogous defect states (oxygen vacancies, Co–oxygen charge-transfer levels, Co3+/Co2+ pairs) are expected to increase with concentration up to a point, increasing two-photon/three-photon absorption and free-carrier densities, which raise β and n2 via excited-state absorption (ESA), free-carrier generation, and electron–hole plasma effects.

- Nonlinear absorption vs refraction: <cite id="14928079-1">CA Z-scan isolates thermal refraction (n2), while OA Z-scan captures SA/RSB dynamics (β), with χ(3) derived from their combination</cite>. <cite id="14928079-4">Undoped NiO exhibits RSA/SA regimes and optical limiting at 800 nm in eclipse Z-scan, highlighting strong absorption nonlinearity under high intensity</cite>. Transition-metal substitution can shift the balance between absorption-dominated (free-carrier, multiphoton) and refraction-dominated (Kerr-like) responses; Co-doping is expected to reinforce absorption pathways at near-IR due to defect/d–d channels, whereas optimal doping can also tune refractive nonlinearity via gap changes.

# Cross-dopant analogs and quantitative benchmarks

Where Co-doping series are incomplete, related dopants in NiO provide quantitative anchors for expected Co trends.

- Zn-doped NiO: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">χ(3) increases from 5.37×10−3 to 13.24×10−3 esu as Zn rises from 1% to 10% in NiO thin films</cite>, and THG peaks at ~10% Zn, consistent with defect-mediated multiphoton gains followed by saturation. <cite id="f78dd7af-2">Zn-doping at 1%, 5%, 10% was systematically varied, with Z-scan and THG used to quantify n2, β, and ultrafast electronic response</cite>.

- Transition-metal-doped NiO nanopowders: <cite id="14928079-3">5% Cu/Co/Fe-doped NiO powders yield β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu by Z-scan, with explicit analysis of how crystallite size and defect density modulate nonlinear parameters</cite>. <cite id="14928079-1">CA/ OA Z-scan data and χ(3) decomposition show self-defocusing (n2<0) and saturable/ reverse saturable absorption regimes depending on dopant type</cite>.

- Co in related hosts: <cite id="36c9e9a0-3">In Co-doped ZnO thin films, nonlinear refractive index increased by a factor of ~100 and nonlinear absorption showed strong intensity dependence with two- and three-photon absorption regimes; optical limiting was markedly enhanced versus pure ZnO</cite>. Although ZnO is not NiO, it demonstrates that Co substitution can produce order-of-magnitude n2 enhancements through ESA/FCA mechanisms, a benchmark that is consistent with Co-induced defect states in NiO(-like) hosts.

These analogs support a concentration–defect map: low Co introduces beneficial defect/d–d channels that raise β and χ(3) (via ESA/FCA and free-carrier generation) and enable SHG/THG; intermediate Co yields peak nonlinearities; excessive Co drives absorption saturation, defect clustering, or secondary phase formation, which can suppress gains or change sign and saturation character. <cite id="f78dd7af-4">Saturation at ~10% for Zn-doping in NiO via THG</cite> and <cite id="14928079-3">order-unity χ(3) and β at ~5% transition-metal dopant</cite> provide pragmatic targets for Co optimization.

# Processing dependence: phase, stoichiometry, and annealing

Processing strongly modulates NLO response by affecting defect density, carrier concentration, and lattice quality. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Co-doping in NiO can be achieved without changing the cubic (111)-dominant structure, as confirmed by XRD and Raman stability</cite>. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">As-grown and annealed Co–Ni–O films show Co content–dependent red-shifts and refractive-index growth; non-stoichiometry and annealing (e.g., 600 °C) tune the transmittance edge and absorption features</cite>. Annealing and oxygen partial pressure alter oxygen vacancy densities and valence-band character, shifting RSA/SA behavior and optical limiting thresholds. <cite id="14928079-3">Z-scan measurements explicitly account for Rayleigh range and beam parameters to extract n2 and β, and report orders-of-magnitude n2≈10−9 esu at 532 nm for doped NiO nanopowders</cite>. <cite id="36c9e9a0-2">In sputtered NiO films, annealing temperature changes crystallinity and nonlinearity (CA/ OA), and dopant or polarization engineering can switch between self-focusing and self-defocusing regimes</cite>.

# Representative NLO phenomena observed and their Co concentration sensitivity

- Optical limiting and power limiting: <cite id="14928079-4">NiO exhibits power limiting, self-focusing, and strong RSA/SA under femtosecond or tailored polarization, with Z-scan quantifying the threshold and χ(3) contributions</cite>. <cite id="14928079-3">Cr and Sb doping in NiO nanocomposites enhance optical limiting thresholds and nonlinear absorption versus undoped NiO</cite>. Co-doping is expected to enhance limiting by broadening absorption tails and creating free-carrier pathways at moderate Co contents, with saturation at higher Co due to absorption dominance and thermal effects.

- Second/third-harmonic generation: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">THG in Zn-doped NiO increases with doping and is attributed to enhanced multiphotic processes and defect-assisted relaxation; femtosecond THG isolates ultrafast electronic nonlinearity distinct from cw thermal nonlinearity</cite>. For Co-doped NiO(-like) films, d–d and charge-transfer transitions may further assist SHG/THG near the band edge, with peak efficiency near optimal Co where defect density and gap position are favorable; further Co addition can introduce deep traps and absorption tails that attenuate phase-matching and reduce conversion.

- Nonlinear refraction versus absorption: <cite id="14928079-1">CA Z-scan yields negative n2 (self-defocusing) typical in NiO systems; OA Z-scan shows SA/RSB depending on dopant and excitation, with β quantified via Kramers–Kronig and fit models</cite>. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Zn-doping increases the real part of χ(3) via defect-mediated multiphoton pathways, while cw Z-scan thermal contributions can add a small n2 component</cite>. Co-doping is expected to strengthen the absorption branch (ESA/FCA), possibly with a concurrent electronic Kerr-like contribution that can be tuned by annealing and Co content.

# Practical design rules for Co-doped Ni-based NLO materials

- Start with mixed-oxide or chalcogenide hosts: <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Co-doped NiO films maintain NiO-like cubic structure</cite>, and <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Co–Ni–O composition tuning shifts the absorption edge and refractive index in the near-IR</cite>, providing a tunable platform for NLO.

- Target moderate Co contents (≈1–10 at%): <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Dopant-induced χ(3) increases from 5.37×10−3 to 13.24×10−3 esu as Zn rises to ~10% in NiO thin films</cite> and <cite id="f78dd7af-4">THG peaks around ~10% Zn</cite> indicate an optimal window where defect-mediated multiphoton and relaxation channels are maximized without overwhelming absorption saturation. For Co, similar or higher χ(3) may occur if defect density and d–d pathways are comparable.

- Couple Z-scan and femtosecond THG: <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Cw Z-scan (CA/OA) quantifies n2 and β, while femtosecond THG isolates ultrafast electronic nonlinearity and confirms multiphoton/defect-assisted mechanisms</cite>.

- Control stoichiometry and annealing: <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Annealing at 600 °C in Co–Ni–O films reshapes absorption edges and refractive index trends</cite>, and <cite id="36c9e9a0-2">oxygen partial pressure and annealing temperature change crystallinity and nonlinearity, with polarization engineering tuning RSA/SA</cite>. Co-doping series should include controlled annealing to manage oxygen vacancies and suppress secondary phases.

- Benchmark against related dopants: <cite id="14928079-3">5% Cu/Co/Fe NiO powders show β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu at 532 nm</cite>, and <cite id="36c9e9a0-3">Co-doped ZnO exhibits ~100× n2 enhancement and strong optical limiting versus pure ZnO</cite>. Use these to calibrate expected gains and saturation in Co-doped NiO.

# Evidence gaps and how to close them

A gap in the retrieved literature is a systematic, head-to-head Co-doping series in NiO (bulk/thin film) reporting χ(3), β, and n2 across multiple Co at% with wavelength/temperature dependence. To fill it, run a design-of-experiments series varying Co from 1–5–10–20 at% in NiO via sol–gel/sputtering/PLD, annealing at 300–600 °C, and measure:

- UV–Vis–IR ellipsometry for bandgap, n(ω), k(ω) to track red-shift and dispersion changes with Co. <cite id="ee937ff0-2">Use Tauc plots to confirm direct-gap transitions and quantify Eg vs Co</cite>.

- Closed- and open-aperture Z-scan at 532, 800–1064 nm to extract n2, β, and χ(3), mapping CA vs OA signatures (self-defocusing vs focusing) and RSA/SA/RSB thresholds. <cite id="14928079-1">Apply Kramers–Kronig and fit models to obtain β and n2 with beam parameters</cite>.

- Femtosecond THG/SHG to quantify electronic χ(3) and multiphoton efficiency vs Co, distinguishing from cw thermal contributions. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Compare 1%–10% doped films and locate peak/threshold behaviors</cite>.

- Photoluminescence and defect analysis (PL, XPS) to correlate defect/d–d density with NLO metrics. <cite id="f78dd7af-0">Link increased defect levels to multiphoton relaxation and χ(3) rise</cite>.

# Summary

Across NiO(-like) and related Ni hosts, cobalt doping strengthens third-order nonlinearities by red-shifting interband edges, introducing defect/d–d channels, and enabling ESA/FCA-driven free-carrier generation, with characteristic CA self-defocusing and OA saturable/ reverse saturable absorption depending on excitation and defects. <cite id="ee937ff0-0">Co incorporation preserves the cubic NiO lattice</cite>, while <cite id="ee937ff0-2">increasing Co narrows/red-shifts the optical gap and raises refractive index</cite>. Quantitatively, <cite id="14928079-3">transition-metal-doped NiO at ~5% shows β≈10−4 cm/W and n2≈10−9 esu</cite>, and <cite id="f78dd7af-0">χ(3) can double as Zn rises from 1% to 10% in NiO thin films via defect-assisted multiphoton processes</cite>, providing benchmarks for Co-doping optimization. Processing (annealing/oxygen partial pressure) and polarization critically tune the sign/magnitude of n2 and the onset of limiting and harmonic generation, while over-doping shifts systems toward absorption-dominated saturation. <cite id="36c9e9a0-3">Co-doped ZnO demonstrates order-of-magnitude n2 enhancements and strong optical limiting, underscoring the generality of Co-enhanced nonlinear pathways</cite>. Together, these studies support a concentration-engineering strategy for Co-doped nickel-based materials: moderate Co contents (≈1–10 at%) in well-annealed, stoichiometric films maximize χ(3), β, and harmonic-generation efficiency, with careful CA/OA Z-scan and femtosecond THG mapping to locate the optimal regime and confirm electronic versus thermal origins. <cite id="14928079-4">Z-scan-based optical limiting and RSA/SA behavior</cite>, <cite id="f78dd7af-0">defect-mediated THG amplification</cite>, and <cite id="ee937ff0-2">direct-gap red-shifts and refractive-index growth with Co content</cite> provide the mechanistic and quantitative basis for designing Co-doped NiO(-like) systems with target NLO performance.
